# Iddhikathā (Ps 3.2)

**ID:** Ps 3.2  
**Section:** Paṭisambhidāmagga (ps)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Iddhikathā  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0517m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0517m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Iddhikathā* ("Discussion of Psychic Powers") constitutes the second treatise of the third section (*vagga*) and the twenty-second treatise overall in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* [Frauwallner 1995; Gethin 2001]. Formulated in the characteristic Abhidhamma-style catechism of the work, the chapter opens with analytical interrogations defining psychic power and its foundations: "What is psychic power? How many psychic powers are there? How many planes of psychic power, how many bases, how many steps, how many roots are there?" (*kā iddhi? kati iddhiyo? iddhiyā kati bhūmiyo, kati pādā, kati padāni, kati mūlāni?*) [Frauwallner 1995; Norman 1983].

The treatise expounds a comprehensive ten-fold typology of psychic or supernormal powers (*iddhi*), including power through determination or resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*) and power through transformation (*vikubbanā-iddhi*) [Bodhi 2003; Fiordalis 2008; Gethin 2001]. It provides detailed instructions on the four bases of spiritual power (*iddhipāda*), elucidating the mind's control over material phenomena—such as traveling invisibly to the Brahmā realm by compelling and directing the body through consciousness [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012; Gethin 2001]. Throughout this exposition, arahants renowned for particular psychic feats are listed by name without background narrative, presuming the reader's prior familiarity with early Buddhist legends [Norman 1983].

The *Iddhikathā* builds upon earlier sutta passages concerning spiritual potency, sharing formulas with the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51), the *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), the *Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta* (MN 77), and the *Kevaṭṭa Sutta* (DN 11) [Norman 1983].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Mentioned in: AN 6.1 Paṭhamaāhuneyyasutta; Mnd 13 Mahābyūhasuttaniddesa; Cnd 8 Mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddesa; DN 33 (PTS DN iii 207) Saṅgīti Sutta; MN 140 (PTS MN iii 237) Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta; DN 10 (PTS DN i 204) Subha Sutta; MN 77 (PTS MN ii 1) Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta; DN 2 (PTS DN i 47) Sāmaññaphala Sutta; Ps 1.1 Ñāṇakathā; MN 152 (PTS MN iii 298) Indriyabhāvanā Sutta; SN 6.14 Aruṇavatīsutta

**Sources**

- [Frauwallner 1995] Erich Frauwallner, Studies in Abhidharma Literature and the Origins of Buddhist Philosophical Systems (1995) — Documented the opening catechetical questions of the Iddhikathā and its structural place in the text.
- [Gethin 2001] R. M. Gethin, The Buddhist Path to Awakening (2001) — Noted the treatise's enumeration of ten kinds of iddhi and treatment of iddhipādas as chapter XXII of the work.
- [Norman 1983] K. R. Norman, Pāli Literature (1983) — Noted the sutta basis of the chapters and the bare mention of arahants possessing psychic powers.
- [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012] Nyanaponika Thera and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Abhidhamma Studies (2012) — Discussed the chapter's teaching on the mind directing the body to the Brahma-world.
- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Referenced specific discussions of transformation power (vikubbanā-iddhi) and bodily buoyancy at Patis II 205 and 209.
- [Fiordalis 2008] David V. Fiordalis, Miracles and Superhuman Powers in South Asian Buddhist Literature (2008) — Discussed adhiṭṭhāna and vikubbana as members of the tenfold classification of iddhi shared with the Visuddhimagga.
